title: CCDV-F Mock Exam #2
description: Full-length 53-question simulation for Claude Certified Developer - Foundations (120 minutes).

questions.prompt: A code-review platform's orchestrator agent receives a large pull request touching 40 files across a frontend and a backend service. The orchestrator delegates the frontend files to one subagent and the backend files to another, each running in its own context window, then synthesizes their findings into one report. What is the main architectural benefit of this manager/supervisor pattern over having a single agent review all 40 files itself?

options.text: It guarantees the review will be more accurate, since subagents run a specially hardened variant of the model that is incapable of making mistakes or missing issues in the code it reviews.
It keeps each subagent's context focused on a relevant subset of files, avoiding a single bloated context window while enabling the two reviews to proceed independently.
It removes the need for the orchestrator to use any tools at all, since dispatching work to subagents and collecting their findings happens automatically without any tool calls from the orchestrator.

It allows the subagents to share one continuous context window with the orchestrator, so the full 40-file diff and all intermediate reasoning remain visible to every participant without needing to be summarized.

questions.explanation: Delegating to subagents with isolated context windows lets each one focus on a coherent slice of work without the full 40-file diff crowding out reasoning space, while the two reviews can proceed independently — this is the core value of manager/supervisor decomposition. Subagents run the same underlying model and are not error-free, so option A is false. The orchestrator still needs tools to dispatch work and collect results, so option C is wrong. Subagents operate in separate context windows and report back rather than sharing the orchestrator's context, so option D is incorrect.

questions.prompt: A Python team evaluating agentic abstraction frameworks such as PydanticAI and Strands for a new internal tool wants to understand what these frameworks typically provide beyond calling the Claude API directly. Which two of the following are accurate benefits such frameworks commonly provide?

options.text: Type-safe or schema-validated structured inputs/outputs for tool calls and agent responses, reducing manual parsing and validation code.
A pre-built abstraction for defining agents, tools, and (in some frameworks) multi-agent orchestration, so teams don't have to hand-roll the same agent-loop boilerplate for every project.

Guaranteed elimination of hallucinated or incorrect tool calls at the framework level, since the schema validation built into frameworks like PydanticAI and Strands catches and prevents any wrong tool call before it executes.

Automatic, cost-free scaling of the underlying model's context window beyond its documented limit, since frameworks like PydanticAI and Strands transparently page conversation history in and out to extend how much the model can see.

questions.explanation: Frameworks like PydanticAI, built around Pydantic-style validation, and Strands emphasize type-safe or schema-validated outputs and reusable agent/tool/orchestration abstractions, saving teams from reimplementing the same boilerplate — matching options 1 and 2. No framework can guarantee a model never produces an incorrect tool call, only make errors easier to catch and validate, so option 3 is false. No abstraction framework increases a model's actual context window, which is a model-level property, so option 4 is false.

questions.prompt: Which signal best indicates that a failed request should not be retried?

options.text: The response took longer than usual
The error indicates a malformed request rather than a transient condition
The same request failed once before
The account is near its spending limit

questions.explanation: A client error means the request itself is wrong, and repeating it unchanged cannot succeed. Latency (A) and a single prior failure (C) are consistent with transient faults, and a spending limit (D) is an operational matter rather than a property of the request.

questions.prompt: A request fails with an authentication error after working for months. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A transient service fault
The prompt became too long
A credential that expired, was rotated, or lost its permissions
The model was deprecated

questions.explanation: Authentication failures point at the credential rather than the payload. A transient fault (A) presents differently, and neither prompt length (B) nor deprecation (D) produces an auth error

questions.prompt: You call Claude on Google Cloud Agent Platform (Vertex). Which statement is true?

options.text: You pass `model` in the JSON body exactly like api.anthropic.com
The model is in the endpoint URL; `anthropic_version` goes in the body
You must use WebSockets
Fast mode is included on every Vertex model

questions.explanation: Agent Platform puts the model in the URL. Fast mode is not a Vertex default. No WebSockets requirement.

questions.prompt: Every request shares a 4K-token policy in `system`, then a short user question. What cuts input cost most?

options.text: Files API
A `cache_control` breakpoint at the end of the stable policy
Raising `max_tokens`
Switching to WebSockets

questions.explanation: Prefix cache on the stable policy. Files API is not a system-prompt cache. `max_tokens` is output. No WebSockets.

questions.prompt: Many products must call the same CRM with the CRM's OAuth. Prefer:

options.text: A one-off custom tool in a single app only, copied six times
An MCP server
A skill that pretends to be the CRM
Putting the CRM password in `CLAUDE.md`

questions.explanation: Shared enterprise + its auth → MCP. Skills do not execute CRM OAuth. Passwords do not belong in `CLAUDE.md`.

questions.prompt: You upload a 40-page PDF and ask 5 different questions about it across 5 separate requests. What's the most efficient approach?

options.text: Re-upload the PDF as base64 each time
Upload once via the Files API and reference by `file_id` in each request
Use the Batch API
Convert the PDF to an image first

questions.explanation: Files API is upload-once, reference-many. Re-uploading wastes tokens. Batch is about volume, not file reuse. Images are the wrong format for a 40-page PDF.

questions.prompt: A production integration receives an HTTP 200 response whose message has `stop_reason: "refusal"`. The team's error middleware only inspects HTTP status codes, so the response text was passed downstream as valid output. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Add `refusal` to the retriable set and retry with exponential backoff until the model complies.

Raise the refusal to the caller and log it, without silently retrying — it is a content decision by the model, not a transient fault, and status-based classification will never catch it because the HTTP layer returned 200.
Treat it as valid output, since a 200 status is authoritative.
Automatically rephrase the prompt and resubmit, keeping the retry invisible to the caller.

questions.explanation: A refusal arrives as HTTP 200 with `stop_reason: "refusal"`: a content decision, not a transient fault. Raise and log it; never silently retry it and never pass it downstream as valid output.

questions.prompt: A retry wrapper's log for one incident shows three responses in sequence: a 429 with `retry-after: 7`, a 500, and a 401. Which handling policy is correct?

options.text: Retry all three with exponential backoff — every failure deserves the same policy so behavior is predictable.

Honor the 429's `retry-after` before retrying, retry the 500 with exponential backoff plus jitter under a cap, and fail fast on the 401 — it is terminal, and retrying an identical bad credential wastes the budget while hiding the real problem.
Fail fast on all three and surface them to the caller; retries belong in the load balancer.
Retry the 401 first since auth systems recover quickly, then the 429, then the 500.

questions.explanation: Classify per status: honor `retry-after` on 429, exponential backoff with jitter under a cap on 5xx, fail fast on terminal statuses like 401 — an identical retry of a bad credential changes nothing and hides the real problem.

questions.prompt: A developer is handling a streamed response that includes a tool_use block. The tool call's input arrives as fragments across many content_block_delta events. When is it safe to parse the input and execute the tool?

options.text: After each delta, parsing incrementally so execution can begin as early as possible
At content_block_start, since the block opens with its name, id, and input
Only after content_block_stop for that block, because the accumulated JSON string is not valid until the block closes
After the first message_delta event, which signals the input is stable

questions.explanation: Tool-call inputs arrive as a partial JSON string spread across deltas and are not valid JSON until content_block_stop closes the block; parsing or executing earlier chokes on malformed JSON or runs with half the arguments missing.

questions.prompt: A second team picks up an agent template labeled "reusable" from a prior engagement. The constructor contains `repo_path="/home/acme/checkout-service"` baked into the code, and the team cannot adapt the template without editing the loop itself. Which change correctly packages the template for reuse?

options.text: Move the repository path into a constants block at the top of the same file
Accept the repository path as a function parameter so each engagement configures the value instead of editing the code
Remove the repository path entirely and have the agent detect the repository at runtime
Fork the template per customer so each copy carries its own hardcoded path

questions.explanation: The hardcoded repo_path is the defect; a reusable template takes the customer-specific value as a parameter so the next team configures the asset instead of editing the code. That is the difference between a template that runs and a template that reuses.

questions.prompt: A team on a regulated engagement is applying lifecycle gates to a Claude application. Which statement correctly describes how a gate works?

options.text: Gates apply only at the final production release, after all engineering work is complete
A gate is an optional documentation checkpoint a team may skip under deadline pressure
A gate is the point in the operate phase where guardrails are first added

The team does not move from design to build until the platform satisfies the residency requirement, and does not move toward full production until the new version clears the eval against the pinned baseline

questions.explanation: A gate is a decision to move from one phase to the next, and it is where a regulated engagement keeps control: no design-to-build move until the platform satisfies residency, and no promotion to production until the eval clears the pinned baseline.

questions.prompt: A B2B analytics SaaS platform team needs a report-generation assistant to analyze a 70-page compliance report directly, including its layout and any embedded tables, rather than manually extracting the text first. What is the best-fit integration approach?

options.text: Manually OCR the PDF into plain text and discard the original layout before calling Claude.
Refuse the request, since Claude cannot process document files.
Pass the PDF directly to Claude as a document content block so it can reason over the full document.
Split the PDF into individual words and send them as a list.

questions.explanation: Claude supports document/file input directly, so PDFs can be passed as a content block and analyzed natively — including layout and tables — without a separate manual extraction step.

questions.prompt: A hospital system's patient-portal engineering team needs a clinical intake assistant to compare two images (e.g., before-and-after screenshots) in a single evaluation. What is the correct way to structure the request?

options.text: Convert both images to base64 and concatenate the strings before sending as one image block.
Claude can only accept one image per request, so the two must be evaluated in separate calls with no shared context.
Stitch the two images into a single file outside the API and hope Claude infers there were originally two.
Include both images as separate content blocks within the same message so Claude can reason over both together.

questions.explanation: Multiple images can be included as separate content blocks in one message, letting Claude directly compare or reason across them in a single call.

questions.prompt: While integrating a report-generation assistant, a B2B analytics SaaS platform team sees a request fail with HTTP 429 and a rate-limit error. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Treat it as a permanent failure and stop calling the API for this feature entirely.
Silently swallow the error and return an empty response to the user.
Immediately retry the exact same request in a tight loop as fast as possible.
Back off and retry after a delay (ideally with exponential backoff and jitter), respecting any provided retry guidance.

questions.explanation: A 429 indicates a rate limit was hit — the correct response is backing off (typically exponential backoff with jitter) and retrying, not hammering the API or giving up permanently.

questions.prompt: A hospital system's patient-portal engineering team wants application logic in a clinical intake assistant to branch correctly depending on why generation ended — for example, executing a tool when Claude requests one versus simply displaying the final answer. Which field should the application inspect?

options.text: The HTTP status code alone, which is always 200 regardless of how generation ended.
The length of the response text, inferring intent from character count.
The response's stop_reason field, which distinguishes cases like end_turn, tool_use, max_tokens, and stop_sequence.
The current system time, to guess whether a tool call is likely.

questions.explanation: stop_reason tells the application why generation stopped (e.g., tool_use vs end_turn vs max_tokens), and is the correct signal for branching application logic — not status code, text length, or guesswork.

questions.prompt: A B2B analytics SaaS platform team needs a report-generation assistant to stop generating cleanly at a specific delimiter the application relies on for parsing, rather than truncating mid-thought. What feature addresses this?

options.text: Removing the system prompt so output is shorter.
stop_sequences, which end generation as soon as a specified string is produced.
Increasing temperature so Claude naturally stops earlier.
Reducing max_tokens until the delimiter happens to land at the cutoff.

questions.explanation: stop_sequences let the application specify exact strings that, once generated, cleanly end the response — the right tool for a reliable, application-defined stopping point.

questions.prompt: A healthcare administration team is building a Claude-powered intake assistant. The business requirement states that patient conversation data must not be retained by the LLM provider beyond what is needed to generate a response, and the deployment must fit within the hospital's existing AWS compliance boundary. Which infrastructure requirement follows most directly from this business requirement?

options.text: Call Claude through Amazon Bedrock (or Claude Platform on AWS) with the organization's data-retention settings configured for zero/minimal retention, keeping the integration inside the hospital's existing AWS compliance boundary.

Use the first-party Claude API directly with 1-hour prompt cache TTLs to reduce cost, since caching is purely a performance optimization and does not change the provider's underlying data-retention commitments.

Store full conversation transcripts in a data lake indefinitely so compliance staff can audit them at any time, treating long-term retention itself as the mechanism that satisfies the hospital's compliance obligations.
Use the Message Batches API so patient intake data can be processed in bulk overnight, since batching requests together is what keeps the integration inside the hospital's compliance boundary.

questions.explanation: Routing through Bedrock/Claude Platform on AWS with retention configured to the required minimum keeps the integration inside the existing AWS compliance boundary and satisfies the retention requirement. Option B focuses on cost, not retention or compliance boundary. Option C directly violates the stated requirement by retaining data indefinitely. Option D addresses latency tolerance, not compliance or retention.

questions.prompt: A Python web service handles many concurrent chat requests, each of which calls the Claude Messages API and waits several seconds for a response. Using the synchronous Anthropic() client with blocking calls inside request handlers causes the service to fall over under moderate load. What is the most appropriate fix?

options.text: Switch to the asynchronous AsyncAnthropic() client and await calls within an async request-handling framework, so the event loop can serve other requests while waiting on I/O.

Increase the number of synchronous worker threads without bound whenever load rises, since blocking calls inside request handlers only become a scaling problem once the thread count exceeds some fixed, predictable threshold.

Reduce max_tokens on every outgoing request so that each Claude API call returns faster and blocks the synchronous worker thread for less wall-clock time, allowing more requests to be handled per thread overall.

Move all Claude API calls out of the application server and into the database layer so the network latency executes during query processing instead, effectively hiding it from the request-handling application code.

questions.explanation: The synchronous client blocks the thread for the duration of a network call; switching to the async client and awaiting it inside an async framework lets the process serve other requests concurrently, which is the standard fix for I/O-bound concurrency problems. Unbounded thread growth (B) doesn't scale and wastes resources. Reducing max_tokens (C) degrades output quality without fixing the architectural bottleneck. Moving calls into the database layer (D) is architecturally incoherent.

questions.prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS platform lets each customer configure a custom system prompt for their own Claude-powered chatbot instance. A security review must confirm that Tenant A's custom system prompt and conversation history can never be visible to, or reused in, a request made on behalf of Tenant B. Which architectural boundary is most important to enforce here?

options.text: Each tenant's requests must be built exclusively from that tenant's own isolated system prompt and conversation history; request-building code must never merge or cache context across tenant boundaries, and cache keys/session state must be scoped per tenant.

The Claude API automatically isolates data between different customers of the same company by tracking the source IP address and account credentials of each incoming request, so the platform does not need to implement any additional tenant-scoping logic of its own.

Store all tenants' conversation histories together in a single shared in-memory array for efficiency, and rely on the model's own reasoning to keep each tenant's turns separate by inferring context from message content rather than enforcing a strict data boundary in code.

Use the same prompt cache breakpoint and cache_control markers for every tenant's requests, because cache_control markers are inherently scoped to the account making the call and automatically prevent cached content from crossing between different tenants.

questions.explanation: Tenant isolation is entirely an application-layer responsibility: request construction, session state, and cache scoping must all be kept per-tenant. Option B is false; the Claude API has no concept of an application's own tenants or IP-based isolation for this purpose. Option C is exactly the kind of design that would leak one tenant's data into another's context. Option D is false; cache_control markers carry no tenant awareness on their own.

questions.prompt: Your team pins model versions in production. What is the primary reason?

options.text: Pinned models are cheaper
Pinning increases the context window
Pinning is required by the API
Model updates can change behavior, so upgrades become deliberate, evaluated changes rather than surprises

questions.explanation: Pinning makes model behavior a controlled dependency so upgrades pass through evaluation

questions.prompt: On Claude Opus 5, sending `temperature=0.7` in a request does what?

options.text: Reduces randomness as expected
Returns a 400 error — sampling parameters are removed on current models
Is silently ignored
Increases cost

questions.explanation: Sampling params are removed on Opus 5 / Fable 5 / Opus 4.8 / 4.7. A 400 is the point, not a silent ignore.

questions.prompt: A team splits a tightly coupled refactoring task across a lead agent and five parallel subagents. The bill roughly triples, latency barely improves, and quality is flat. What explains the outcome?

options.text: The subagents' prompts were uncached; prompt caching would have made the fan-out cost-neutral.
Five subagents is below the threshold where parallelism pays; ten or more would show gains.

Each subagent burns tokens in its own context — a multi-agent run costs many times a single chat (roughly 15x in Anthropic's reported case) — and the multiplier only pays off when the task splits into independent parts, which a tightly coupled refactor does not.
The lead model was too small to coordinate; upgrading only the lead recovers the quality.

questions.explanation: Every subagent spends tokens in its own context (~15x a normal chat in Anthropic's reported case), and the multiplier only pays off on tasks that decompose into independent parts. A tightly coupled refactor leaves subagents serialized on each other — fan-out cost, no fan-out benefit.

questions.prompt: A developer on the newest Claude models wants deeper reasoning on hard requests. According to the module, how is reasoning depth tuned?

options.text: By setting a fixed budget_tokens value, the recommended control on the newest generations.
By switching to a different model, since reasoning mode and model choice are the same setting.
By raising the temperature so the model explores more possibilities.
Through adaptive thinking's effort setting — the model decides when and how much to think — while the older budget_tokens control is deprecated and returns a 400 error on the newest generations.

questions.explanation: On current models the reasoning mode is adaptive thinking, tuned with an effort setting rather than a fixed token budget; budget_tokens is deprecated and returns a 400 error on the newest generations.

questions.prompt: A team runs an overnight classification backfill over a large dataset. No user is waiting on the results, and every request carries the same long, fixed system prompt. Which configuration best fits the workload?

options.text: Stream every response so results arrive as fast as possible
Submit the work through the Message Batches API for roughly a 50% cost reduction, and add prompt caching on the stable prefix so the two savings compound
Fan the dataset out across parallel subagents so the job finishes within the hour
Move the job to the most capable model tier so fewer retries are needed

questions.explanation: A non-urgent, no-user-waiting job is exactly what the Message Batches API is for (~50% cost reduction for asynchronous processing), and prompt caching compounds the saving because the long fixed system prompt recurs across requests. Streaming optimizes perceived latency for a user in the loop, which this job has none of.

questions.prompt: A hospital system's patient-portal engineering team is deciding whether a batch classification job for a clinical intake assistant over patient intake forms needs extended thinking enabled. The task is a simple, well-defined label assignment with little ambiguity. What is the right call?

options.text: Skip extended thinking for this simple, well-defined task — the added latency and cost aren't justified when reasoning depth isn't the bottleneck.
Extended thinking is required for all batch jobs regardless of task complexity.
Extended thinking replaces the need for model tier selection entirely.
Enable extended thinking for every request, since more reasoning budget is always better regardless of task difficulty.

questions.explanation: Extended thinking adds latency and cost for deeper reasoning — worthwhile for genuinely hard, ambiguous problems, but not justified for simple, well-defined classification tasks.

questions.prompt: A CI pipeline needs to invoke Claude Code as one step of an automated pull-request check: it must run without any human present, exit after producing a single result, and print output that a downstream script can parse programmatically. Which invocation best satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Launch the normal interactive `claude` REPL inside the CI job and have the pipeline script pause and wait for a human operator to type a response at the prompt before the step can complete and the job can continue.

Run `claude -p "<prompt>" --output-format json` so Claude Code executes headlessly in a single pass, prints one structured, machine-readable response, and then exits immediately without waiting for any further interactive input.

Run `claude --resume` in the CI job to reattach to and continue a previous interactive session, then parse its resumed transcript afterward, since resuming an existing session is the standard way to obtain a single scripted result inside automation.

Enable auto-mode so file edits and tool calls are accepted automatically without prompting, then start the standard interactive session inside the CI job and let it run to completion before the pipeline reads the terminal output.

questions.explanation: Headless mode (`-p` with `--output-format json`) runs Claude Code non-interactively for exactly one turn and emits structured output suited to scripting, which is exactly what an unattended CI step needs. The interactive REPL blocks waiting for input, which cannot work in an unattended pipeline. --resume is for continuing a prior interactive session, not for a fresh one-shot scripted call. Auto-mode only changes how permission prompts are handled inside an interactive session; it does not make the session non-interactive or scriptable.

questions.prompt: A teammate proposes an autonomous agent for a pipeline whose five steps are identical for every input. What is the strongest technical objection?

options.text: A known, fixed path does not need model-chosen control flow; deterministic orchestration is cheaper, testable, and auditable
Agents are unsupported in production
Agents cannot call tools reliably
The pipeline would need a larger context window

questions.explanation: Autonomy is justified when the path is unknown. A fixed path belongs in deterministic code that can be tested

questions.prompt: Under the Managed Agents (CMA) model, where does `model`/`system`/`tools` configuration live?

options.text: On the session (`sessions.create`)
On the agent (`agents.create`) — sessions only reference the agent by ID
On the environment
Split evenly between agent and session

questions.explanation: Agent holds config. Session references the agent ID. Environment is the container template, not the prompt.

questions.prompt:
An agent loop is implemented as:

```
while True:
    resp = client.messages.create(..., tools=tools, messages=history)
    # ...?
```

Which statement correctly describes how the loop should decide to continue or stop?

options.text: Continue while `stop_reason` is `tool_use` — execute the requested tools, append the results as `tool_result` blocks in a **user** turn, and call again; exit when the model returns `end_turn` (with a max-iteration guard against runaways).
Continue until the model returns an empty content array, which is the completion signal.
Continue while `stop_reason` is `tool_use`, appending each `tool_result` as an **assistant** turn since the application produced it.
No loop is needed — the API executes requested tools server-side and returns the final answer in one call.

questions.explanation: The loop continues while `stop_reason` is `tool_use`: execute the tools, return results as `tool_result` blocks in a **user** turn, call again; exit on `end_turn`, with a max-iteration guard. Tool results always ride in the user role, and the Messages API never executes your tools for you.

questions.prompt: A B2B analytics SaaS platform team is building an internal assistant for the account-management inbox where requests vary widely, and the assistant must decide whether to look something up, ask a clarifying question, synthesize an answer, or stop, based on intermediate results. Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: A single prompt that forbids the assistant from ever asking a clarifying question.
A nightly batch job that processes all requests the same way regardless of content.
An agent loop that plans, takes an action, observes the result, and decides whether to continue or stop.
A fixed workflow using the exact same steps for every request.

questions.explanation: An agent loop (plan → act → observe → decide) fits open-ended tasks that require dynamic choices and reacting to intermediate results — a fixed sequence can't be enumerated in advance here.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team is designing an orchestration for a returns-processing assistant where a complex request should be broken into specialized sub-tasks (e.g., one for research, one for drafting, one for review), each best handled with its own focused context and tools. What pattern fits best?

options.text: A single agent handling the entire request in one undifferentiated context with every tool available at once.
An orchestrator that delegates specialized sub-tasks to dedicated subagents and synthesizes their results.
Ignoring task specialization entirely and relying on a bigger context window instead.
A fixed workflow with no ability to delegate any part of the task.

questions.explanation: An orchestrator–subagents pattern fits well when a complex task naturally splits into specialized sub-tasks, each better served by its own focused context and tools, with results synthesized centrally.

questions.prompt: A hospital system's patient-portal engineering team gives an agent a complex, multi-part goal for a clinical intake assistant (e.g., investigate an issue, propose a fix, and draft a summary). What is the recommended approach inside the agent's own reasoning?

options.text: Randomly choose which part of the goal to address first with no particular order.
Decompose the goal into ordered sub-goals, tackling them in sequence and checking progress along the way.
Attempt the entire multi-part goal in one single, undivided step with no intermediate structure.
Refuse the task because it has more than one part.

questions.explanation: Multi-step task decomposition — breaking a complex goal into ordered sub-goals and checking progress — is the recommended approach, mirroring good workflow design inside an agent's own loop.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team has a task for a loan-underwriting assistant where one LLM call drafts an answer and a second, separate LLM call critiques it against explicit criteria, looping until the draft passes. Which workflow pattern does this describe?

options.text: A single-call workflow with no iteration.
Prompt chaining with no evaluation step.
A pure routing pattern with no generation involved.
An evaluator-optimizer loop, where a generator and an evaluator iterate until the output meets the criteria.

questions.explanation: A generator producing a draft and a separate evaluator critiquing it against explicit criteria, iterating until it passes, is the evaluator-optimizer workflow pattern.

questions.prompt: A production service calling the Messages API starts intermittently receiving HTTP 529 responses with `error.type: "overloaded_error"` during a traffic spike, alongside normal 200 responses for most requests. The service has no custom retry logic and relies on the Anthropic SDK's defaults. Which statement about handling this correctly?

options.text: Treat every 529 overloaded_error as a fatal, non-retryable failure and immediately surface an error back to the user-facing request without any retry attempt, since an overloaded_error response means the request body itself was malformed in a way that cannot succeed no matter how many times or when it is resent.

Do nothing extra beyond the SDK's built-in handling — the Anthropic SDK already retries 529 (as well as 429 and 5xx) responses with exponential backoff by default, so occasional 529s appearing in logs during a traffic spike are expected and typically self-resolve without any code changes.

Switch permanently to a different, less capable model for all future requests, since a 529 overloaded_error indicates that the specific model version being requested has been deprecated and is no longer being served by the API.

Immediately resend the exact same request in a tight loop with no delay between attempts, in order to beat other tenants' traffic back to available capacity before the overload condition clears on its own.

questions.explanation: `overloaded_error` (529) is a retryable, transient capacity error, and the Anthropic SDKs automatically retry 429/408/409/5xx and 529 with exponential backoff (default max_retries=2) — so seeing some in logs during a spike is expected, and the default behavior already handles it. Option A is wrong because 529 is about server capacity, not a bad request (that would be 400/invalid_request_error). Option C is wrong because overload is transient and has nothing to do with model deprecation (which returns 404). Option D is wrong because retrying instantly with no backoff worsens congestion and ignores the `retry-after` guidance the API provides.

questions.prompt: Which change most improves output that is correct but inconsistently formatted?

options.text: Providing an example of the exact output required
Raising the temperature
Asking for the output to be neat
Using a larger model

questions.explanation: An example defines the target unambiguously, which is what formatting consistency needs. Higher temperature (B) increases variance, a vague adjective (C) does not specify, and a larger model (D) does not know your format

questions.prompt: Context is growing. Old tool blobs are noise. You still need the conversation to continue. Which pair is correct?

options.text: Context editing *prunes* stale blocks. It does not summarize
Compaction *summarizes*. You must echo the full `response.content` back
The memory tool only exists inside one request
You should put a changing timestamp in the system prompt so the model stays fresh

questions.explanation: Memory persists *across* sessions if you store it. Timestamps in the system prompt break cache and add drift.

questions.prompt: A developer builds a support ticket processor with the system prompt "You are a support ticket processor. Extract the key information from the ticket below." Claude returns plausible but inconsistent output — sometimes prose, sometimes JSON with varying field names — and the downstream parser keeps breaking. What structural piece is missing from the prompt?

options.text: Extended thinking, so the model reasons about the ticket before extracting fields
An output constraint specifying the exact JSON structure, field names, allowed values, and an instruction to return nothing else
A higher max_tokens value so the full extraction is never truncated
Additional paragraphs describing each ticket category in more detail

questions.explanation: The defect is a missing output constraint: the prompt never specified the JSON structure, exact field names, allowed values, or the instruction to return nothing else, so Claude returns plausible but inconsistent output that breaks the downstream parser.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform's backend team wants a returns-processing assistant's response to start immediately with valid JSON, with no preamble like 'Sure, here is the JSON:' in front of it. What technique addresses this directly?

options.text: Asking politely in the system prompt and hoping the preamble doesn't appear.
Post-processing every response to strip an unpredictable amount of leading text.
Lowering max_tokens until the preamble is cut off.
Prefilling the start of Claude's response (e.g., with an opening brace) so generation continues directly into the desired format.

questions.explanation: Prefilling the assistant turn (starting the response for Claude, e.g. with an opening brace) is the direct technique for forcing generation to continue straight into the desired format without preamble.

questions.prompt: A B2B analytics SaaS platform team is building a feature in a report-generation assistant that requires solving a genuinely hard multi-step reasoning problem, and wants the model's answer to be more reliable by reasoning explicitly before concluding. What prompting technique fits best?

options.text: Repeating the question multiple times in the same prompt.
Chain-of-thought prompting — explicitly asking Claude to reason step by step before giving the final answer.
Asking for the shortest possible answer with no reasoning shown.
Removing all context to force a faster guess.

questions.explanation: Chain-of-thought prompting — asking the model to reason step by step before answering — is well suited to improving reliability on genuinely hard, multi-step reasoning problems.

questions.prompt: A developer building a long-running chat application is surprised when a request fails after many turns, even though each individual user message was short. Which statement correctly explains what counts against a model's context window?

options.text: Only the newest user message's text counts toward the context window, since prior turns in the conversation are cached separately by the API and no longer occupy any of the token budget once a response has been generated for them.

The context window is strictly an output-token cap describing the maximum length of the model's generated response, while the input side, including the system prompt and full conversation history, can be arbitrarily long without limit.
The context window is a shared token budget across the entire request: the system prompt, full conversation history sent with the request, and the generated output all count against it.

Because each API call is a fresh, stateless request, the context window automatically resets to zero every time, so however much conversation history the client appends to the messages array, it never actually consumes any of the token budget.

questions.explanation: The context window is a single shared budget covering the system prompt, all messages sent as input, and the tokens the model generates in response — as history grows, less room remains for the response. Options A, B, and D each describe a way the window could be circumvented that does not reflect how the token budget actually works.

questions.prompt: A finance team wants to model the actual dollar cost of a Claude-powered feature, knowing that input tokens and output tokens are priced differently. What should the application read from the API response to compute the cost of a given request?

options.text: The `stop_reason` field returned with the response, since Anthropic populates this field with the exact dollar amount billed for that specific request based on the model and content involved.
The response's token usage information (input token count and output token count), multiplied by the model's per-token input and output prices respectively.

The character length of the prompt and completion strings, since Claude's tokenizer maps exactly one character to one token, making character counts a reliable direct substitute for token counts in cost math.
The wall-clock HTTP response time recorded by the client, since Anthropic bills requests based on how many seconds or milliseconds the model spent processing before returning the completed response.

questions.explanation: Cost is calculated from the actual input and output token counts reported in the response's usage data, multiplied by the model's published per-token rates for input and output respectively. `stop_reason` (A) describes why generation stopped, not cost; characters and tokens (C) are not a fixed 1:1 mapping; and response latency (D) has no bearing on token-based billing.

questions.prompt: An MCP server is added and the agent's success rate falls. What should be checked first?

options.text: Whether the new tools overlap with existing ones and have distinguishable descriptions
The server's uptime
The model version
The network latency

questions.explanation: A new tool surface most often degrades selection through overlap and unclear descriptions. Uptime (B) and latency (D) present as errors or slowness, and the model did not change (C)

questions.prompt: In one assistant turn, Claude emits three `tool_use` blocks for three independent client-side tools. What's the correct way to return results?

options.text: Three separate user messages, one per result
One user message containing all three `tool_result` blocks
Ignore the extras and only answer the first
Ask the user which one to answer

questions.explanation: One user message, all `tool_result` blocks. Splitting them trains the model not to call in parallel. Dropping two of three breaks the protocol.

questions.prompt: In a session trace, the assistant turn issues a tool_use block with id="toolu_01" for get_account_balance. The next user turn returns a tool_result with tool_use_id="toolu_02" and the correct balance content. The following request fails with invalid_request_error: "tool_result block references unknown tool_use_id." What is the targeted fix?

options.text: Update the description on get_account_balance to add an exclusion condition
Correct the tool_use_id on the tool_result block so it matches the id issued in the assistant turn
Add a required array to the tool's input_schema so account_id cannot be omitted
Move the tool_result block into an assistant-role turn, since the application generated its content

questions.explanation: The API matches tool_use and tool_result blocks by id, not position, so tool_use_id="toolu_02" references a tool_use block that does not exist. The fix is returning the result with tool_use_id="toolu_01"; tool_result blocks correctly belong in the user role.

questions.prompt: A developer must package a working MCP server as a reusable accelerator so other teams can install it in new environments. What does correct packaging require?

options.text: Hardcode the scopes the original engagement used so the server behaves identically everywhere
Ship only the server binary, since MCP tool behavior is self-describing at runtime
Document each tool input and let the installing team set the scope, so the server installs into a new environment without code edits
Bundle the original customer's credentials so the server works out of the box

questions.explanation: Correct MCP server packaging documents each tool input and lets the installing team set the scope, so the server installs into a new environment without code edits. Hardcoded scopes or bundled credentials tie the package to the original engagement.

questions.prompt: An engineering team builds a coding assistant that must search and reason across a very large monorepo to answer a single user question. If the main agent itself runs dozens of file reads and greps to find the answer, its own context fills with raw search results, most of which are irrelevant to the final answer. Which architecture best addresses this?

options.text: Keep the search-and-explore work inside the main agent itself, having it run every file read and grep, then manually delete older tool-result messages from its own context once space runs low.
Dispatch the search-and-explore work to one or more subagents that return only a condensed finding, so the main agent's context stays isolated from the raw intermediate search output.
Raise the main agent's temperature so its sampling process can better tolerate and average over a context window cluttered with large volumes of irrelevant raw search results.
Require the user to supply the exact file path and line number before the agent starts, so it never needs to run its own searches or manage the resulting output in context.

questions.explanation: Delegating exploratory work to subagents isolates the noisy intermediate tool output in the subagent's own context and returns only a distilled result to the orchestrator, a standard context-isolation pattern for multi-step agentic workflows. Manually deleting messages is fragile and doesn't scale, and the main agent still has to run and read every search. Temperature has no effect on context size or clutter. Requiring the user to pre-locate the answer defeats the purpose of building an agent to do that work.

questions.prompt: What is the appropriate way to give an integration access to a database?

options.text: Provide full credentials so the model can handle any request
Provide read and write access but instruct the model to avoid writes
Expose only the specific operations the task requires, scoped to what it may touch
Provide access through a tool with no schema so it stays flexible

questions.explanation: Least privilege bounds the consequences of any mistake or manipulation, and it is enforced outside the prompt. Full credentials (A) and instruction-based restraint (B) rely on behavior rather than control, and an unscoped tool (D) removes the boundary.

questions.prompt: A support agent must not email customers. Which pair is the secure design?

options.text: Do not expose `send_email` in that agent's tool list
Rely only on "never email" in the system prompt
Use a hook / `always_ask` if an email-like tool must exist for admins
Put the SMTP password in the system prompt so the model can send "only if needed"

questions.explanation: Least privilege plus a deterministic gate. Prompt-only and secrets-in-prompt are the exam traps.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup's platform engineering team needs to send records containing customer SSNs and account numbers to Claude as part of a loan-underwriting assistant's processing. What is the most responsible approach?

options.text: Send the data as-is with no consideration of data-handling policy, since it's only used internally.
Avoid the feature entirely rather than considering any data-handling safeguards.
Ask Claude in the prompt to 'forget' the sensitive data immediately after responding, and treat that as sufficient.
Redact or minimize sensitive identifiers where possible and follow the organization's data-handling and retention policies for what must be sent.

questions.explanation: Responsible handling of sensitive data means minimizing/redacting identifiers where possible and following the organization's actual data-handling and retention policy — an in-prompt request to 'forget' data is not a policy control.

questions.prompt: An internal Claude-powered agent lets employees ask natural-language questions and calls a get_customer_record tool to fetch data from the CRM. Different employees are authorized to see different subsets of customer records depending on their role. Which design best prevents an employee from viewing records outside their authorization?

options.text: Provision the agent with a single shared CRM credential that has full read access to every record, and rely on a system-prompt instruction telling it to only surface records the employee may see.
Have the tool implementation validate the requesting employee's identity and permissions server-side on every call, and scope the returned data to only what that employee is authorized to access.
Have employees type their own role and access level into the chat, and pass that self-reported claim directly to the get_customer_record tool as the basis for deciding which records to return.
Load the entire customer database into the model's context window at the start of every session, giving it full visibility into all records so it can reason about who should see what.

questions.explanation: Authorization must be enforced server-side in the tool layer, independent of the model's reasoning, so results are scoped to what the authenticated caller may access. Relying on system-prompt instructions (option A) or self-reported claims (option C) is bypassable, and loading the full database into context (option D) both fails to enforce access control and creates unnecessary exposure of sensitive data.

questions.prompt: An engineer builds an internal support agent and gives it five separate tools — get_file, read_file, fetch_document, load_text, and retrieve_file_content — that all wrap nearly identical file-reading logic, differing only in minor details such as whether pagination is supported. In testing, Claude frequently calls the wrong tool or supplies mismatched parameters. Which change best addresses the problem?

options.text: Add even more specialized tools for every remaining file-access variation — a paginated reader, a streaming reader, a binary reader — so each distinct need has its own dedicated, narrowly scoped tool.

Lengthen each of the five tools' descriptions with more detailed usage examples and parameter explanations, while keeping all five tools in place since each still covers a slightly different scenario.

Randomize the order in which the five tools are listed in the tools array on each request, on the theory that varying the presentation order will stop Claude from repeatedly fixating on the same wrong tool.
Consolidate the overlapping tools into a single, clearly described tool with optional parameters (e.g., a page parameter) to cover the real differences between them.

questions.explanation: Keeping the tool set small and unambiguous — here, consolidating near-duplicate tools into one well-described tool with parameters for the real differences — removes the functional overlap causing Claude to pick the wrong tool. Adding more specialized tools increases ambiguity rather than resolving it. Lengthening descriptions without removing overlap doesn't fix the root cause, since the tools still do the same thing. Reordering tools in the request has no bearing on functional overlap.
